story.headline: Gold jumped back above $3,600 and US stock futures rose about 2% overnight after Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned the Fed against hiking too far. The dollar slipped only slightly from its 19-month high.

reads.policy: A December Fed hike is still expected, but bets on a bigger half-point move vanished after Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned against hiking too far. The European Central Bank and Bank of England are also expected to hike, while Australia's weakening economy makes another Reserve Bank of Australia hike unlikely. US rates still look set to rise further than most, which keeps supporting the dollar.
reads.growth: Australian business activity is shrinking at its fastest pace in more than five years, another blow to the Aussie. New Zealand shoppers, by contrast, spent far more than expected over the summer quarter, which helps the kiwi. Euro-area, UK and US business surveys for November come out on Monday.
reads.inflation: Inflation is still well above target almost everywhere, which keeps most central banks leaning toward hikes. Australian firms say price rises are slowing, which eases pressure on their central bank. Wednesday's US core inflation figures are the big test for the Fed this week.
reads.risk: US stock futures bounced overnight after last week's AI-driven slide, which cooled demand for the yen and the franc. Asian shares still fell, and Asian governments stepped in to steady their markets. Weekend threats in the Gulf, including reported mines near the Strait of Hormuz, keep some caution in place.
reads.tot: Oil held steady overnight as markets waited to see whether Gulf threats turn into lost supply, which leaves the Canadian dollar without fresh support. Gold bounced back strongly, which helps the Aussie. Energy buyers such as Japan and the euro area still benefit from oil well below this year's highs.
reads.positioning: The latest weekly figures show hedge funds have turned slightly against the dollar after betting on it, while still betting against the euro, the kiwi, the franc and, most strongly, the Canadian dollar. They still bet on the pound and the Aussie, where big long-term investors take the opposite side. Where the two groups disagree, a surprise could set off a fast unwind.
reads.fiscal: France's debts, flagged by the European Central Bank as a risk, keep weighing on the euro. Record US government borrowing still keeps long-term US borrowing costs high, though they slipped below 5% as money rushed into bonds during last week's stock slide.

fed.summary: The Federal Reserve held rates on October 28 with two officials voting to hike, and most officials now expect more hikes. Bets on a bigger half-point move in December have vanished after a stock slide and a warning from the Treasury, but a quarter-point hike is still the likely next move.
fed.priced: December: quarter-point hike very likely. Half-point hike no longer expected.
fed.why: US inflation is running at about twice the Fed's 2% goal. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned the Fed against hiking too far, and a falling stock market gives officials a reason to go carefully.
fed.watch: US business surveys on Monday, November 23 at 8:45 AM CT and core inflation for October on Wednesday, November 25 at 7:30 AM CT. The decision is December 9.

boc.summary: The Bank of Canada raised rates to 2.50% in October and said more may be needed. October inflation held at 3.1% with core prices near 2%, so a December hike now looks less likely than not.
boc.priced: December: hold more likely, with a hike a bit under even odds.
boc.why: Energy is lifting headline inflation, but core prices are calm and the economy is shedding jobs, so the bank can afford to wait.
boc.watch: Governor Tiff Macklem speaks Tuesday, November 24 at 11:25 AM CT, and oil prices. The decision is December 9.

rbnz.summary: The Reserve Bank of New Zealand held at 2.75% in October in a narrow vote. Rising unemployment has made a December hike less certain, but a jump in shop sales in the third quarter strengthens the case for one.
rbnz.priced: December: hike possible but not fully expected.
rbnz.why: Inflation pressures and stronger spending argue for a hike, while unemployment at its highest since 2015 argues for waiting. Governor Anna Breman gave no clear signal on December in her latest speech.
rbnz.watch: The official election result on Friday, November 27 and the next dairy price auction. The decision is December 9.

ecb.summary: The European Central Bank held at 2.50% in October and a December hike is widely expected. Euro-area inflation is confirmed at 4.0%, but the euro sits just under $1.10 as US rates rise faster.
ecb.priced: December: hike widely expected, possibly the last for a while.
ecb.why: Euro-area inflation is about double the bank's goal and core prices are firming. Weak factories and France's debts, which the bank's stability report singled out, limit how far it can go.
ecb.watch: Euro-area business surveys on Monday, November 23 at 3:00 AM CT and the accounts of the October meeting on Thursday, November 26 at 6:30 AM CT. The decision is December 17.

boj.summary: The Bank of Japan holds at 1.25%, far below other major banks, and is expected to hike in December. Japan's October inflation came in a touch below forecast but stayed above the bank's 2% goal, which keeps that hike likely.
boj.why: Inflation has stayed above 2% for a second month, and the weak yen keeps pushing up import and food prices. The small summer contraction is the main reason to wait.
boj.watch: The bank's own core inflation measure on Tuesday, November 24 at 11:00 PM CT, Tokyo's November inflation figures on Thursday, November 26 at 5:30 PM CT, and any sign Japan steps in near 160 yen. The decision is December 18.

rba.summary: The Reserve Bank of Australia raised rates to 4.85% on November 3, the highest among the major banks. Job losses and a business survey showing the fastest shrinking in more than five years suggest rates have peaked, and the Aussie is near its lowest in a year.
rba.priced: December: a hold expected. Some bets on cuts in 2027 are building.
rba.why: Inflation is still too high for most of the board, but the economy is clearly weakening and firms say price rises are slowing. That makes a further hike unlikely and puts the timing of a first cut in question.
rba.watch: Australian inflation for October on Tuesday, November 24 at 6:30 PM CT. The decision is December 8.

boe.summary: The Bank of England raised Bank Rate to 4.00% on November 5 and said more may follow. UK shoppers spent more than expected in October, which supports a second hike in December, but the pound sits close to its lowest this year as US rates rise faster.
boe.priced: December: a second hike more likely than not.
boe.why: High fuel costs from the Middle East conflict keep UK inflation near twice the bank's goal. Spending held up in October, although much of it was food stockpiling that may not last.
boe.watch: UK business surveys on Monday, November 23 at 3:30 AM CT, then talks by chief economist Huw Pill on Monday at 7:00 AM CT and Megan Greene on Tuesday, November 24 at 6:30 AM CT. The decision is December 17.

snb.summary: The Swiss National Bank holds its rate at zero and can sell francs if they get too strong. Low Swiss inflation means no hike is in sight.
snb.why: Swiss inflation is low, so the bank has no reason to raise rates and some room to cut if the franc climbs.
snb.watch: Any flare-up in stock markets or the Gulf that sends money into the franc. The decision is December 10.

GBP.summary: The pound sits at the top of the board because UK interest rates are among the highest of the eight. Steady core inflation trimmed bets on another hike, and it trades close to its lowest this year.

AUD.summary: The Aussie sits second on the board, thanks to the highest interest rates among the major central banks. A shrinking economy and October job losses suggest those rates have peaked, and it trades near its lowest in a year.

USD.summary: The dollar sits third on the board. High and rising US interest rates support it, while large budget deficits weigh a little. It trades just below its highest since April 2025 as a quarter-point Fed hike in December is still expected.

NZD.summary: The kiwi sits fourth, in the middle of the board. Firm dairy prices and a jump in shop sales help, but doubts over a December rate hike have kept it near its lowest since 2020.

EUR.summary: The euro sits fifth, just below the middle of the board. Cheaper oil helps the euro area, but France's debts and rates below most of the others hold it back. It trades close to its weakest in about 18 months.

CAD.summary: The Canadian dollar sits sixth, in the lower half of the board. Falling oil prices hurt Canada's exports, and recent Canadian data has mostly missed forecasts. It is near its weakest against the US dollar in more than a year.

JPY.summary: The yen sits second from the bottom because Japanese interest rates are far below the others. A likely December Bank of Japan hike and last week's stock slide gave it some support, but the dollar still trades near 159 yen.

CHF.summary: The franc sits at the bottom of the board. Swiss interest rates are the lowest of the eight and inflation is too low to need higher rates. It gains mainly when fear in markets sends safe-haven money its way.
